newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plunges into final weekend of campaign.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plunges into final weekend of campaign.

text.p: A huge crowd chanting "Clinton, Clinton" welcomed President Bill Clinton to New Mexico's second largest city on Friday night as he plunged into the final weekend of his campaign for re-election.

The throng included American Indians in colourful native costumes and feather headdresses, leathery-looking farmers in jeans and cowboy hats, Hispanic-Americans who make up much of the population here and thousands of excited young people.

In size and enthusiasm, it was typical of the kind of crowds Clinton has attracted all along the campaign trail this year, starting with his whistlestop train trip to the Democratic convention in August. The crowds for Republican Bob Dole consistently have been much smaller.
"Su Voto Es Su Voz" (Your Vote Is Your Voice) said one sign at the rally, reflecting its Hispanic flavor. "Yes, You Can Count On Us," said another placard waved by a Clinton supporter.

"He kissed me on the cheek! He hugged me! I was reaching my arms out too!" screamed Gina Misquez, 17, a Las Cruces High School senior, after Clinton worked the ropeline shaking hands following the rally.

In spite of the electricity the president has generated in his quest for a second term, Clinton campaign aides expect a low voter turnout for Tuesday's election. "Maybe lower than 51 percent," said one official.
Fifty-five percent of the U.S. electorate cast ballots in 1992 when Clinton defeated then-President George Bush.
"A low turnout could hurt us, but not enough to change the outcome," the official said, implicitly confirming that the Clinton camp believes victory on Tuesday is a foregone conclusion.

Clinton visited the southwest after wrapping up his campaign for California's 54 electoral votes -- one fifth of the 270 he needs to win a second term -- with a call for a sweeping overhaul of campaign finance laws including a ban on contributions by non-citizens.

Trying to defuse a controversy about Democratic fundraising tactics, he insisted that he and his party had "played by the rules" in collecting campaign money. But he called for changes that he said in the past were blocked by Dole, a 35-year veteran of Congress.

Clinton did not deal directly with questions about his links to John Huang, a Democratic fundraiser who reportedly raised a lot of cash from powerful Asian business interests and enjoyed frequent access to the White House.
"Everybody knows the problems of campaign money," Clinton told a rally in Santa Barbara. "There's too much of it, it takes too much time to raise and it raises too many questions."

Clinton's schedule on Saturday included a rally at the Alamo in San Antonio with his wife Hillary, an airport stop in his hometown of Little Rock, Ark. and a final pre-election visit to Florida. While Dole is campaigning non-stop in a final push, Clinton's relatively relaxed pace showed his optimism about Tuesday's outcome.

Another sign of Clinton's confidence was his decision to cancel an election-eve visit to California, where the election is likely to be decided. Clinton had planned a wind-up a rally in Los Angeles on Monday night, but will instead concentrate his final vote-getting efforts in Ohio, Kentucky and Iowa.
